title: 2027 Toyota Tundra: Did Toyota Fix the Engine? What We Know So Far

scenes.text: The Toyota Tundra keeps eighty percent of its value after five years, and it is one of the trucks most likely to reach two hundred fifty thousand miles. But the same truck was ranked last for reliability by one of the biggest truck sites in America, because of engine failures that sometimes meant a whole new engine. For twenty twenty-seven, Toyota says the problem has been addressed. Here is what changed, what did not, and whether you should believe it.
scenes.caption: 2027 TUNDRA: DID TOYOTA FIX IT?

scenes.text: The Toyota Tundra is a strange truck to talk about, because it has two reputations at once. On one side, the numbers on resale and longevity are among the best of any truck. On the other side, there is a known engine problem on the twenty twenty-two to twenty twenty-four trucks. And now there is a new model year, with new styling, a bigger screen, and a hybrid with more power. We will go through all of it, with sources.
scenes.caption: TWO REPUTATIONS AT ONCE

scenes.text: We used Pickup Truck Talk's two articles on the twenty twenty-seven Tundra, published in July, plus CarGurus from September ninth and Kelley Blue Book for the price estimates. For resale, iSeeCars. For longevity, the iSeeCars study as reported by Work Truck Online. For sales, the Pickup Truck Talk table. A key point. Toyota has not published prices or on-sale dates for the twenty twenty-seven Tundra in these sources, so every price in this video is an estimate.
scenes.caption: PRICES ARE ESTIMATES. TOYOTA HAS NOT PUBLISHED THEM.

scenes.text: There is a twist in every part of this. One engine is unchanged, and that is the story. One hybrid makes more power than any other Tundra. One feature requires a subscription. And one list of complaints was not addressed. Stay with me, because the last twist is about a sentence in a review that the readers did not accept.
scenes.caption: FOUR TWISTS

scenes.text: Change number one is the engine, and the answer is that there is no new engine. According to Pickup Truck Talk, the twenty twenty-seven Tundra keeps the three point four liter twin-turbocharged V six, either alone or in the i-Force Max hybrid. The V eight is not coming back, and the old five point seven liter V eight, which made three hundred eighty-one horsepower and four hundred one pound-feet, is gone for good.
scenes.query: Toyota Tundra V6 twin turbo engine
scenes.caption: NO NEW ENGINE. NO V8.

scenes.text: Now the problem. According to the same article, failures on certain twenty twenty-two to twenty twenty-four trucks were traced to machining debris trapped in the number one crankshaft main bearing. That could cause knocking, rough running, no-starts, power loss, or complete engine failure. Toyota introduced an improved main bearing and other manufacturing changes, and recall documents say engines built after those changes fall outside the affected production period.
scenes.caption: 2022-2024: DEBRIS IN THE MAIN BEARING

scenes.text: The twist is the remedy. The latest recall repair uses dealer diagnostic software and vehicle operating data to decide whether an engine needs to be replaced. So not every truck gets a new engine. A diagnostic decides. And Toyota says that the manufacturing problem has been addressed. The article adds an important line, which is that buyers must decide for themselves whether enough time has passed to restore confidence.
scenes.caption: REMEDY: DIAGNOSE, THEN DECIDE

scenes.text: A separate Pickup Truck Talk article from January says that a significant number of twenty twenty-two to twenty twenty-four engines were recalled, with no official campaigns published for twenty twenty-five or twenty twenty-six engines for this problem. It does not give a count. And in July, Pickup Truck Talk ranked the Tundra fifth of five full-size trucks for reliability, citing twin-turbo V six failures that in some cases required a complete engine replacement.
scenes.caption: PUTT RELIABILITY RANK: 5TH OF 5

scenes.text: Change number two is the power. The i-Force Max hybrid makes four hundred thirty-seven horsepower and five hundred eighty-three pound-feet of torque, according to Pickup Truck Talk, compared with three hundred eighty-nine horsepower and four hundred seventy-nine pound-feet for the standard V six in most configurations. That is forty-eight more horsepower and one hundred four more pound-feet of torque. The hybrid is the most powerful Tundra.
scenes.caption: HYBRID: 437 HP, 583 LB-FT

scenes.text: And there is a new feature that comes only with the hybrid. A two point four kilowatt inverter, which Pickup Truck Talk calls the most significant change for twenty twenty-seven, with uses for job sites, camping and emergency power. The twist is that Toyota has not yet said where the outlets are, what the operating limits are, or whether it delivers full output while parked. So the feature is real, and the details are not.
scenes.caption: 2.4-KW INVERTER: DETAILS PENDING

scenes.text: Fuel economy, for reference, is a modest part of this truck. KBB's page lists twenty miles per gallon in the city, twenty-four on the highway and twenty-two combined for the powertrain it shows, with a range of nineteen to twenty-two combined across the page. CarGurus lists seventeen to twenty in the city, twenty to twenty-four on the highway, and nineteen to twenty-two combined for twenty twenty-six. These are last year's numbers, and the twenty twenty-seven ratings are not confirmed.
scenes.caption: 2026 MPG: 19-22 COMBINED

scenes.text: Change number three is what you see and touch. The front end is redesigned, with a squared-off look and a stronger vertical grille, and the body-colored mustache trim is gone. There is a new Trailhunter package based on the SR5, with Old Man Emu suspension, Michelin tires, front recovery hooks, underbody protection, Multi-Terrain Select, Crawl Control, a locking rear differential and bronze wheels. Toyota says it is meant to offer an adventure-ready Tundra at a more accessible price.
scenes.caption: NEW: TRAILHUNTER, SR5-BASED

scenes.text: Inside, a fourteen inch screen is standard on every twenty twenty-seven Tundra, replacing the eight inch screen on base trucks. A dash camera is standard, recording twenty second clips. Toyota Safety Sense four point oh is standard, and there is a digital key that works through a phone wallet app. The twist is the key. It requires an active Remote Connect trial or subscription, so a feature you use every day can depend on a service you may have to pay for.
scenes.caption: DIGITAL KEY NEEDS A SUBSCRIPTION

scenes.text: Change number four is what did not change. Pickup Truck Talk notes that the initial announcement did not specifically address cracking plastic panels around the front seats, squeaky brakes, tailgate problems and wind noise. The article says production changes may still have been made, but they were not mentioned. These are small problems compared with an engine, and they are the kind of problems that owners talk about.
scenes.caption: NOT ADDRESSED: PANELS, BRAKES, TAILGATE

scenes.text: And here is the last twist, about that sentence. The reviewer wrote that the recalls over the engine issues are done. The article presents it as the author's opinion, not as a Toyota statement, and the readers' comments dispute it. That is a fair summary of where the Tundra stands. One side believes the problem is behind the truck. The other side does not. Neither can prove it yet, because the newer engines have fewer miles.
scenes.caption: AUTHOR: RECALLS ARE DONE. READERS: NOT SURE.

scenes.text: Now the price, and we will be careful. Toyota has not published twenty twenty-seven prices in the sources we found. CarGurus says that the twenty twenty-six base price was forty-one thousand, two hundred sixty dollars including destination, and that the top Capstone model topped eighty thousand. Kelley Blue Book estimates the twenty twenty-seven SR Double Cab at forty-five thousand dollars, and the Capstone at eighty-four thousand. The KBB numbers are estimates, not Toyota's.
scenes.caption: KBB ESTIMATE: $45,000 TO $84,000

scenes.text: KBB's estimates for the middle of the range are forty-nine thousand, five hundred for the SR5, fifty-three thousand, five hundred for the Trailhunter, fifty-eight thousand for the Limited CrewMax, sixty-six thousand, five hundred for the Platinum, sixty-seven thousand, five hundred for the Tundra 1794 Edition, and seventy-five thousand, five hundred for the TRD Pro. Again, these are estimates. They tell you that the Tundra is expected to cost about what the average full-size truck costs, which was sixty-seven thousand, four hundred forty-six dollars in August.
scenes.caption: ESTIMATES: TRAILHUNTER $53,500. TRD PRO $75,500.

scenes.text: Towing and payload are not confirmed either. CarGurus says that the twenty twenty-six Tundra could tow up to twelve thousand pounds, with a payload of up to eighteen hundred fifty pounds. KBB's page shows eleven thousand, four hundred fifty pounds of towing and sixteen hundred sixty-five pounds of payload, for the configuration it displays. The two sources disagree, probably because they describe different trims. So check the door sticker for the exact truck.
scenes.caption: TOWING: 12,000 OR 11,450 LB?

scenes.text: Now the numbers that made the Tundra's reputation. The truck sold one hundred ten thousand and eighty through nine months of twenty twenty-six, down eight tenths of a percent. In the third quarter, thirty-five thousand, seven hundred twelve, down seven tenths. It is very steady. And iSeeCars shows it keeping eighty and three tenths percent of its value after five years, about eighteen points above the Ram one thousand five hundred, and nineteen above the Ford F-one-fifty.
scenes.caption: TUNDRA: 110,080. RESALE: 80.3%

scenes.text: On longevity, the Tundra is second in the twenty twenty-six iSeeCars study, at twenty-eight point two percent, about two and a half times the truck average. In the earlier edition, it was second too, at forty-seven point nine. So on resale and on lasting, the Tundra is at the top. On reliability, according to Pickup Truck Talk, it is at the bottom. The same truck, and three very different answers.
scenes.caption: LONGEVITY: 28.2%, 2ND IN BOTH EDITIONS

scenes.text: How can all three be true? Because they measure different things. Resale measures what buyers are willing to pay, which includes trust in the brand. Longevity measures how many trucks reach a high mileage, which includes trucks with replaced engines. And the reliability ranking measures problems, recalls and repair cost. A truck can be trusted by the market, last a long time, and still have a serious flaw on some model years. That is what the Tundra is.
scenes.caption: THREE MEASURES, THREE ANSWERS

scenes.text: So who should buy a twenty twenty-seven Tundra? A buyer who values resale, who keeps trucks for a long time, and who accepts that Toyota has said the manufacturing problem has been addressed. Also a buyer who wants a hybrid with real power, and the inverter. And who should wait? A buyer who wants proof. Because a twenty twenty-seven truck has no track record yet, and the twenty twenty-two to twenty twenty-four trucks are the ones with the known problem.
scenes.caption: WHO: LONG-TERM KEEPERS. WAIT: SKEPTICS.

scenes.text: And if you are shopping for a used Tundra, the advice is different. Check the build date of the exact truck, and check whether the recall repair was done. A twenty twenty-two to twenty twenty-four truck that has had a documented repair is a different purchase from one that has not. Ask for the paperwork. A Toyota dealer can look up the recall status with the vehicle identification number, and it takes a few minutes.
scenes.caption: USED TUNDRA: CHECK THE RECALL STATUS

scenes.text: Let us slow down on the recall, because this is the part that confuses people. A recall is not the same as a verdict. It means the manufacturer, or the government, identified a defect that can affect safety or function, and a repair is offered at no cost to the owner. It does not tell you how many trucks actually failed. And it does not tell you whether a repaired truck will last. So the right question is not whether there was a recall. It is whether this exact truck was repaired.
scenes.caption: A RECALL IS NOT A VERDICT

scenes.text: Here is how to check. Every truck has a seventeen character vehicle identification number, found on the driver side of the dashboard and on the door jamb. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration lets you type that number on its recall website and see open recalls for free. A Toyota dealer can also look it up. If a recall is open, the repair is free. If it was done, ask for the paperwork. This takes five minutes, and it matters more than any review.
scenes.caption: CHECK THE VIN: FREE, FIVE MINUTES

scenes.text: Now the question about the hybrid. The i-Force Max has forty-eight more horsepower and one hundred four more pound-feet than the standard V six, and the inverter. But it adds complexity, a battery and electric motor, and the sources we used do not give the extra cost for twenty twenty-seven. So the honest advice is simple. If you tow heavy loads, or want to power tools on a job site, the hybrid makes sense. If you drive mostly on roads with light loads, the standard V six already has three hundred eighty-nine horsepower, and that is plenty.
scenes.caption: HYBRID: WORTH IT FOR TOWING AND POWER

scenes.text: It also helps to read the longevity study carefully. A truck can reach two hundred fifty thousand miles because the engine is excellent, or because an owner replaced the engine and kept driving. The study counts miles, not repair bills. And resale value measures what the market believes today. If the market is wrong about a problem, the price will change later. So use these numbers as signals, not as guarantees, and never as a replacement for checking the exact truck.
scenes.caption: MILES COUNT. REPAIR BILLS DO NOT.

scenes.text: One more point for buyers who finance. A truck that holds eighty percent of its value helps you when it is time to sell or trade. But the price you pay at the start still matters most. At the estimates we saw, a Tundra can cost from forty-five thousand to eighty-four thousand dollars. Every thousand dollars you pay above the average is a thousand dollars you need the resale value to cover. So compare the same trim, the same options, and the same day, across at least three dealers.
scenes.caption: HIGH RESALE DOES NOT REPLACE A GOOD PRICE

scenes.text: So what should you check before you buy a Tundra in twenty twenty-seven? First, the official price and the on-sale date, once Toyota announces them. Second, the warranty for the engine and the hybrid system, in writing. Third, the recall status for any used truck. And fourth, the towing and payload on the door sticker. We put all of this into a checklist, the Twenty Twenty-Seven Truck Buyer's Guide. The link is in the description and in the pinned comment.
scenes.caption: CHECK 1, 2, 3 AND 4
